overview: This map window spans the later Saadian era, the rise of Alaouite rule in the seventeenth century, and the protectorates established in 1912. Its 1650 to 1938 dates are mapping limits, not Morocco’s lifetime.

periods.title: Alaouite rule takes shape
periods.summary: The seventeenth-century dynastic transition was followed by new imperial and commercial building projects.

periods.title: Protectorate period within this map entry
periods.summary: French and Spanish protectorate arrangements reduced Moroccan sovereignty; the monarchy was not abolished.

sections.title: Cities and the people who sustained them

items.text: Moulay Ismail, who reigned from 1672 to 1727, made Meknes his capital. The palace city and older medina were distinct ensembles divided by walls. Their different spaces preserve a ruler’s administrative ambitions alongside an existing urban community.

Meknes’s surviving heritage includes hammams, merchant inns, private houses and large granaries as well as palaces. These buildings span several periods. They make washing, storage, commerce and shelter visible beside royal display; they should not all be assigned to one sultan.

The royal state also relied on coercion. Historian Chouki El Hamel studied registers used under Moulay Ismail to justify enslaving Black Moroccans, including people who had been free. The policy provoked opposition among Muslim scholars; official paperwork could manufacture a claim to ownership rather than prove a just right.

Sultan Sidi Mohamed ben Abdallah, ruling from 1757 to 1790, developed Essaouira as a royal Atlantic port. Its planned fortifications drew on European military design within a Moroccan urban setting. Goods could pass between inland African routes, the coast and European shipping.

Essaouira’s population included Muslim, Jewish and Christian communities and people of different backgrounds. Its port was a meeting place as well as a defensive project. The surviving town preserves the settings of exchange without implying that every resident experienced identical opportunities.

A treaty concluded in 1786 formalised relations with the United States. In 1821, Sultan Moulay Suleiman gave the Americans a building in Tangier for their diplomatic mission. The surviving institutional history shows diplomacy expressed through both written agreements and a very tangible house.

sections.title: Light, food and words at home

items.text: A nineteenth-century batta jug in the Batha Museum held lamp oil. It has a rounded body, narrow neck and pouring lip, and stands only 14 centimetres high. Before an electric light switch, keeping a lamp supplied required small, purpose-made containers like this.

Fez and Meknes potters made these jugs for different markets. Green examples went particularly to southern oasis regions, while urban buyers could obtain more elaborate multicoloured decoration. One familiar vessel shape could be adapted to several customers.

A shallow Fez dish from the first half of the nineteenth century is 40 centimetres across. Dishes of this type served bastila, a filled pie, but this especially symbolic example may have been primarily decorative. A beautiful plate is not proof of the exact meal once eaten from it.

Its blue decoration was painted with cobalt oxide and its yellow with an iron-based pigment. A mosque-like arch frames a word arranged as a mirror image. The dish shows potters combining material knowledge, architectural references and writing on a domestic form.

The dish’s Arabic word is الملك, al-mulk, “sovereignty” or “power,” interpreted by the museum as divine power. It is printed here in ordinary letters; the original is highly stylised, mirrored Kufic. This is an attested object inscription, not a phrase invented for the card.

Later in this entry’s period, the French Protectorate developed a planned capital at Rabat, especially from 1912 to 1930, alongside older urban layers. Its government buildings and neighbourhoods record colonial intervention as well as architectural exchange.

ending.text: The 1912 protectorates limited Moroccan sovereignty without abolishing the monarchy. Independence returned in 1956. The map’s break at 1938 is not a conquest date or the disappearance of Morocco.
